note: Candidate drops "occasionally" from "wrong judgments are occasionally suggested".
replacement: With this moral sentiment, as with our others, the question of its origin is not necessarily connected with the question of its binding force. That Nature has given us a feeling does not by itself justify everything the feeling urges. The feeling of justice might be a peculiar instinct and yet need, like our other instincts, to be controlled and enlightened by a higher reason. We have intellectual instincts, which lead us to judge in a particular way, as well as animal instincts, which prompt us to act in a particular way. There is no necessity that the former be more infallible in their sphere than the latter in theirs. Wrong judgments may occasionally be suggested by the one just as wrong actions are by the other. But it is one thing to believe that we have natural feelings of justice, and another to accept them as an ultimate criterion of conduct. Even so, in point of fact, these two opinions are very closely connected. Mankind are always predisposed to believe that any subjective feeling which cannot be accounted for in some other way is a revelation of some objective reality. Our present object is to determine whether the reality to which the feeling of justice corresponds is one that needs any such special revelation. Is the justice or injustice of an action something intrinsically peculiar, distinct from all its other qualities? Or is it only a combination of certain of those qualities, seen under a peculiar aspect? For this inquiry it is practically important to ask whether the feeling of justice and injustice is itself _sui generis_, like our sensations of color and taste, or is a derivative feeling, formed by a combination of others. It is all the more essential to examine this because people are in general willing enough to allow that, objectively, the dictates of justice coincide with a part of the field of General Expediency. But the subjective mental feeling of Justice differs from the feeling that commonly attaches to simple expediency, and, except in extreme cases of the latter, it is far more imperative in its demands. So people find it difficult to see in Justice only a particular kind or branch of general utility, and they think that its superior binding force requires a totally different origin.

note: Candidate drops "Even" from "Even in slave countries".
replacement: Closely allied to impartiality is the idea of _equality_. It often enters as a component into both the conception and the practice of justice, and many people see it as the essence of justice. But here, even more than elsewhere, different people hold different notions of justice, and the variations always follow their notion of utility. Each person holds that equality is what justice dictates, unless he thinks expediency calls for inequality. Even the defenders of the most outrageous inequality in the rights themselves maintain that the rights of all deserve equal protection. Even in slave countries it is admitted in theory that the slave's rights, such as they are, ought to be as sacred as the master's, and that a tribunal which enforces them less strictly is lacking in justice. Yet institutions that leave the slave hardly any rights to enforce are not deemed unjust, because they are not deemed inexpedient. People who think utility requires distinctions of rank see no injustice in an unequal distribution of riches and social privileges. People who think that inequality inexpedient think it unjust too. Whoever thinks government necessary sees no injustice in the inequality created when a magistrate is given powers that other people lack. Even among the holders of levelling doctrines there are as many questions of justice as there are differences of opinion about expediency. Some Communists consider it unjust to share the produce of the community's labor on any principle but exact equality. Others think it just that those with the greatest needs receive most. Others hold that those who work harder, or produce more, or give more valuable service to the community, may justly claim a larger share of the produce. And the sense of natural justice can plausibly be called on in support of every one of these opinions.

note: Candidate drops "even" from "a rule even of utter selfishness".
replacement: It is no objection to this doctrine to say that when we feel our sentiment of justice outraged, we are not thinking of society at large, or of any collective interest, but only of the individual case. It is common enough, certainly, though the reverse of commendable, to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain. But consider a person whose resentment is really a moral feeling, that is, who considers whether an act is blameable before he allows himself to resent it. Such a person may not say expressly to himself that he is standing up for the interest of society, but he certainly does feel that he is asserting a rule which is for the benefit of others as well as for his own. If he is not feeling this, and is regarding the act solely as it affects him individually, he is not consciously just: he is not concerning himself about the justice of his actions. Even anti-utilitarian moralists admit this. When Kant (as remarked before) propounds as the fundamental principle of morals, "So act, that thy rule of conduct might be adopted as a law by all rational beings," he virtually acknowledges that the interest of mankind collectively, or at least of mankind indiscriminately, must be in the mind of the agent when he is conscientiously deciding on the morality of the act. Otherwise he uses words without a meaning. For it cannot even be plausibly maintained that even a rule of utter selfishness could not _possibly_ be adopted by all rational beings, or that there is any insuperable obstacle in the nature of things to its adoption. To give any meaning to Kant's principle, the sense put on it must be that we ought to shape our conduct by a rule which all rational beings might adopt _with benefit to their collective interest_.
